questions.code: for (int i = 1; i <= n; i += 2) cnt++;
questions.h: Roughly how many times does the loop run? Then drop the constant.
questions.e: It runs about n / 2 times, and constants are dropped: O(n).

questions.code: for (int i = n; i > 1; i /= 2) cnt++;
questions.h: How many times can you halve n before it reaches 1?
questions.e: i is halved each round, so it reaches 1 after about log₂ n rounds.

questions.code:
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
    for (int j = 0; j < 100; j++) cnt++;
questions.h: Does the inner loop depend on n?
questions.e: The inner loop always runs 100 times, a constant. 100 × n is O(n).

questions.h: The two parts run one after the other: add them and keep the biggest term.
questions.e: n + n² steps; keep the biggest term: O(n²).

questions.code:
for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++)
    for (int j = 1; j <= n; j *= 3) cnt++;
questions.h: The inner loop multiplies j by 3 each round.
questions.e: The inner loop multiplies j by 3, so it runs about log₃ n times for each of the n outer rounds.

questions.q: n ≤ 10^6 and the time limit is 1 second. Which complexity is too slow?
questions.h: Square 10^6 and compare it with about 10^8 operations per second.
questions.e: O(n²) would be about 10^12 steps, far above the roughly 10^8 operations per second.

questions.q: What is the extra space of an n × n grid of ints?
questions.h: How many values does an n × n grid store?
questions.e: The grid stores n × n values, so it uses O(n²) memory.

questions.q: A recursive function calls itself n levels deep before returning. How much stack space does it use?
questions.h: How many calls are waiting on the stack at the deepest point?
questions.e: Every call that is still waiting sits on the call stack, so n levels deep is O(n) space.

questions.code:
long long i = 2;
while (i <= n) i = i * i;
questions.h: Write i for a few rounds: 2, 4, …
questions.e: i goes 2, 4, 16, 256, …: it is squared each round, which reaches n after about log log n rounds.

questions.q: Which grows the fastest as n gets large?
questions.e: Exponential growth beats every power of n: 2ⁿ eventually passes n³, n² and n log n.
